newsitem.title: CUBA: Canadian minister sees Cuban tourism, oil sites.
newsitem.headline: Canadian minister sees Cuban tourism, oil sites.

text.p: Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, on a 24-hour trip that has irked the United States, toured economic sites on the communist-ruled island on Wednesday and said Cuba was open to foreign business.
Axworthy was escorted round some oil wells and hotels at Varadero, a picture-postcard beach resort 148 km (90 miles) east of Havana, by deputy president Carlos Lage.

The visit to the oil wells, where Canadian firm Sherrit International is involved in a recovery enhancement programme, and to two hotels in Varadero was intended to give Axworthy a glimpse of changing economic times in Cuba.

"It was informative to find out about developments in tourism and other parts of the economy," he told reporters. "It was interesting to see the range of foreign investment that's taking place and to see there is an openness for foreign investment to come to Cuba."

Canadian firms, particularly in mining and tourism, have led foreign companies in investing in Cuba after the island began a drive to draw foreign capital five years ago. Canada is also a leading trade partner of Cuba and Canadians are the largest group of tourists to visit the island.

This position has placed Canada among the most vocal opponents of the Helms-Burton law, the tougher version of the 35-year-old U.S. economic embargo on Cuba that was approved last year and includes provisions to punish some foreign firms investing on the island.

Sherritt was one of the first firms to be targeted by the law. Its senior executives were barred entry to the United States last year under a provision punishing firms deemed to be benefitting from property nationalised after President Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution.

While Canadian officials have stressed that his one-day visit is not aimed at making any point on Helms-Burton, rather at exploring how Cuba and Canada can develop their ties, the trip has underscored the differences between Ottowa and Washington's Cuba policy.

Speaking to reporters after talks late Tuesday with Castro, Axworthy put some emphasis on Canada's view that to engage in dialogue with Cuba will be more productive as a means of encouraging economic and political reforms than isolating it.

"I don't want to tell you that we are about to have a great breakthrough but it's a work in progress," Axworthy said after meeting Castro for nearly three hours over dinner at the Palace of the Revolution.
He said he raised issues such as human rights and political prisoners with Castro, but did not give details.
Axworthy said Cuban authorities were "prepared to talk to you, as long as you come in a pretty straight-forward way and not hectoring."
His visit was expected to produce a joint declaration on future cooperation on a range of areas, including steps in the area of human rights and governance.
This declaration could be announced later on Wednesday at a news conference before Axworthy leaves for Ottawa.

Axworthy, accompanied by Secretary of State for Africa and Latin America Christine Stewart, is making the highest level visit to Cuba by a Canadian official in two decades. The last high-level visit was by prime minister Pierre Trudeau in 1976.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday that Canada was rewarding Castro by sending its foreign minister to visit the island.
But Axworthy sought to tone down any disagreement, saying Burns later called the Canadian embassy in Washington to say the U.S. did not use these methods but did not oppose them.
